question_text: “The most significant achievement of modern law in India is the constitutionalization of environmental problems by the Supreme Court.” Discuss this statement with the help of relevant case laws. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Constitutionalisation of the environment
topics: Constitutionalisation of the environment
keyPointers: The Court read a right to environment into Article 21
Polluter pays, precaution and public trust became working doctrines
PILs turned a local harm into a constitutional case
The achievement is real, and it is not a substitute for a statute

points.text: The Supreme Court made environmental harm a breach of the right to life, not only a breach of a licence.
Cases such as Subhash Kumar, M.C. Mehta, Vellore and the public-trust line in M.C. Mehta (Span Motel) did this work.
Polluter pays, precaution and absolute liability gave the Court a remedy where the statute was slow.
The limit is that a judgment is case-wise, and enforcement still needs a board, a budget and a law.
Constitutionalisation is the Court's large achievement. It does not retire the need for ordinary environmental law.

question_text: “Right of movement and residence throughout the territory of India are freely available to the Indian citizens, but these rights are not absolute.” Comment. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Movement and residence are not absolute
topics: Movement and residence are not absolute
keyPointers: Article 19 gives the citizen, not every person, this freedom
The Constitution itself lists the limits
Security, public order, a scheduled tribe's land and a public interest can restrict it
A restriction must be a law, and it must be reasonable

points.text: The freedom to move and reside anywhere in India is wide, and it is fenced.
Article 19(1)(d) and (e) belong to citizens.
Article 19(5) allows a reasonable restriction in the interests of the general public or for the protection of a Scheduled Tribe.
An externment order, a curfew under a lawful regime, or a land law that shields tribal land can therefore stand, if the restriction is proportionate.
The right is free inside the territory, and it stops where a stated public interest, by law, begins.

question_text: To what extent, in your opinion, has the decentralisation of power in India changed the governance landscape at the grassroots? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: What decentralisation changed at the grassroots
topics: What decentralisation changed at the grassroots
keyPointers: The 73rd and 74th Amendments created an elected local state
Reservation brought women and excluded groups into the chair
Money, staff and the function list did not follow fully
The landscape changed more in representation than in power

points.text: Decentralisation changed who sits at the local table more than it changed who decides.
Regular elections, reservation and a gram sabha made a local political class that did not exist in this form.
Funds and functions remain tied to the state department and the scheme.
Where a state devolved, local works and local accountability improved. Where it did not, the panchayat is a counter.
The landscape has changed, but the change is uneven and still short of self-government.

question_text: Discuss the role of the Vice-President of India as the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Vice-President as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
topics: Vice-President as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
keyPointers: The Vice-President's working office is the Chair of the Upper House
The Chair runs the sitting and guards the procedure
The vote is a casting vote, not a political lead
The role is of the House, not of the government

points.text: As Chairman, the Vice-President is the presiding officer of the Rajya Sabha.
The Chair decides points of order, maintains the list of business and can adjourn a disorderly sitting.
Bills, resolutions and a member's conduct are handled under the rules the Chair applies.
A casting vote is used only in a tie, and the Chair does not join the government's whip.
The role is to keep the Council of States a deliberating House.

question_text: Discuss the role of the National Commission for Backward Classes in the wake of its transformation from a statutory body to a constitutional body. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: NCBC after it became constitutional
topics: NCBC after it became constitutional
keyPointers: The 102nd Amendment lifted the Commission into the Constitution
Article 338B gives it the powers of a civil court
Inclusion in the Central List now runs through this body
A constitutional status raises the duty, not automatically the result

points.text: The NCBC moved from a law-made body to a body the Constitution requires.
Article 338B mandates it to monitor safeguards, inquire into complaints and advise on the social and economic development of backward classes.
It has civil-court powers for a summons and a document.
Advice on lists is now structurally harder for a government to ignore, though the last word on policy remains political.
The transformation matters because advice on backward classes now comes from a body the Constitution itself protects.

question_text: The Gati-Shakti Yojana needs meticulous coordination between the government and the private sector to achieve the goal of connectivity. Discuss. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Gati-Shakti and public-private coordination
topics: Gati-Shakti and public-private coordination
keyPointers: Gati-Shakti is a map of projects, not a new road by itself
Ministries, states and a concessionaire must use the same plan
The private role is capital, construction and a logistics park
Coordination fails when land, a clearance and a contract run on different clocks

points.text: Gati-Shakti reaches connectivity only if the public plan and the private builder share one timeline.
The platform is meant to stop a rail, a road, a port and a power line being planned in ignorance of each other.
Private capital builds stations, freight parks and last-mile links, but it will not come without a clear contract and a land that is actually free.
A state delay or a ministry that will not share its layer breaks the whole corridor.
The goal is coordination. Without it the scheme is a dashboard.

question_text: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 remains only a legal document without intense sensitisation of government functionaries and citizens regarding disability. Comment. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Disability rights need more than the Act
topics: Disability rights need more than the Act
subTopics: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act
keyPointers: The 2016 Act widened rights and the list of disabilities
A right that the clerk and the neighbour do not accept is unused
Sensitisation is the bridge from the gazette to the ramp and the job
The comment is fair: law is necessary and not sufficient

points.text: The Act creates the right. Sensitisation decides whether a person can use it.
Reservation, accessibility and a reason-based distinction mean little if an office still treats disability as charity.
Officials who do not know the law delay certificates, buildings and a reasonable accommodation.
Citizens who stare, exclude or design only for themselves undo the public duty the Act states.
Without that change of habit the Act stays a document.

question_text: Reforming the government delivery system through the Direct Benefit Transfer Scheme is a progressive step, but it has its own limitations too. Comment. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: Direct Benefit Transfer and its limits
topics: Direct Benefit Transfer and its limits
keyPointers: DBT cuts a leak by paying the person, not the middleman
It needs a bank account, a number and a working authentication
Exclusion of the eligible is the new failure
Progressive in design, limited by the last mile

points.text: DBT is progressive because it replaces a leaky chain with a credit to the beneficiary.
Ghost names and a diverted sack become harder.
The person without a reliable account, a mobile link or a fingerprint match is now excluded by the reform itself.
A delay, a wrong seeding and a weak grievance system reproduce the old hardship in a digital form.
The step is real. Its limit is that a transfer is only as fair as the list and the authentication.

question_text: ‘India is an age-old friend of Sri Lanka.’ Discuss India's role in the recent crisis in Sri Lanka in the light of the preceding statement. (Answer in 150 words)
topic: India and Sri Lanka's recent crisis
topics: India and Sri Lanka's recent crisis
subTopics: India and the Sri Lanka crisis
keyPointers: The friendship claim was tested by a balance-of-payments collapse
India answered with credit, fuel, food and currency support
The help was also about a stable neighbour and an open sea lane
Friendship here was timely assistance without taking over the politics

points.text: India treated the Sri Lankan collapse as a neighbour's emergency, and acted like one.
Credit lines for fuel and essentials, currency support and supplies arrived when reserves had failed.
This matched an old relationship and a current interest: a stable island, and no vacuum for another power.
India did not, and could not, replace Sri Lanka's own reform of tax, debt and the political crisis.
The role fits the claim of friendship if it is read as first help, not as ownership.

question_text: Do you think that BIMSTEC is a parallel organisation like the SAARC? What are the similarities and dissimilarities between the two? How are Indian foreign policy objectives realized by forming this new organisation? (Answer in 150 words)
topic: BIMSTEC and SAARC
topics: BIMSTEC and SAARC
keyPointers: BIMSTEC is not a copy of SAARC with a new name
Both are regional, and both include India
SAARC is stalled by India-Pakistan politics; BIMSTEC leaves that out and adds South East Asia
India uses BIMSTEC to keep a regional agenda moving

points.text: BIMSTEC looks parallel to SAARC, but it was built to go around SAARC's blockage.
Both group neighbours for trade, connectivity and a shared problem. SAARC is South Asia including Pakistan. BIMSTEC is the Bay, linking South Asia to ASEAN without Pakistan.
SAARC's summit diplomacy froze. BIMSTEC lets India pursue connectivity, a blue economy and Act East with willing partners.
It does not replace SAARC's unfinished South Asian business.
Indian objectives are met by having a regional table that still meets.

question_text: Discuss the procedures to decide the disputes arising out of the election of a Member of the Parliament or State Legislature under The Representation of the People Act, 1951. What are the grounds on which the election of any returned candidate may be declared void? What remedy is available to the aggrieved party against the decision? Refer to the case laws. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Election disputes under the RPA 1951
topics: Election disputes under the RPA 1951
keyPointers: An election dispute goes to a High Court, not to the House
The 1951 Act lists the grounds for voiding a return
Corrupt practice, a wrong acceptance of a nomination and a bad count are core grounds
Appeal lies to the Supreme Court

points.text: The Representation of the People Act, 1951, takes an election dispute out of the legislature and into a court.
An election petition is filed in the High Court of the state, within the limitation the Act sets.

The returned candidate's election can be declared void for a disqualification, a nomination wrongly accepted or rejected, a corrupt practice, or a result materially affected by improper acceptance, rejection or a wrong count.
The High Court tries the petition with the powers of a trial.
The aggrieved party appeals to the Supreme Court. The courts have treated the right to challenge as statutory, so the procedure in the Act is the procedure.
The remedy against the decision is that appeal, not a second political vote.

question_text: Discuss the essential conditions for exercise of the legislative powers by the Governor. Discuss the legality of re-promulgation of ordinances by the Governor without placing them before the Legislature. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Governor's ordinance and re-promulgation
topics: Governor's ordinance and re-promulgation
keyPointers: The Governor legislates by ordinance only when the House is not sitting
There must be a circumstance that needs immediate action
The ordinance is temporary and must be laid before the legislature
Re-promulgation to avoid the House is an abuse, and the Court has said so

points.text: The Governor's legislative power is an emergency pen, not a second assembly.
Under Article 213 the House or Houses must not be in session, and the Governor must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary to act at once.
The ordinance has the force of an Act and dies if it is not laid and approved within the period the Constitution sets.
It cannot do what the state legislature cannot do, and a few matters need the President's instruction.
In D.C. Wadhwa the Court held that repeated re-promulgation, without placing the ordinance before the legislature, subverts the democratic process and is unconstitutional.
Re-promulgation as a method of bypassing the House is not a legal use of the power.

question_text: “While the national political parties in India favour centralisation, the regional parties are in favour of State autonomy.” Comment. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: National parties, regional parties and autonomy
topics: National parties, regional parties and autonomy
keyPointers: The contrast is a tendency, not a law of parties
A national party in office at the Centre defends the Union instrument
A regional party is built on a state grievance and a state vote
Coalition years forced the national party to bargain

points.text: The statement catches a real tilt, and it overstates it.
National parties draw a vote from many states and staff the Union, so they defend a strong Centre, governors, and central schemes.
Regional parties win on language, a regional hurt or a state service, so they argue for the State List, fiscal room and a say in national coalitions.
The same national party, when it sits only in a state, can talk like a regional one. A regional party inside the Union cabinet defends a central law that helps its state.
Federal practice since the 1990s is this bargain, not a clean two-party theory.
The comment is a useful first cut. Office, not the label alone, decides who wants the Centre strong.

question_text: Critically examine the procedures through which the Presidents of India and France are elected. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: How India and France elect a President
topics: How India and France elect a President
keyPointers: Both are indirect, and they are indirect for different reasons
India's President is elected by an electoral college weighted to federalism
France's President is directly elected by the people in two rounds
The procedure reveals the kind of president each constitution wants

points.text: The two procedures produce two different presidencies.

India: elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the state legislative assemblies vote. The value of a vote is weighted so that the Union and the states, and large and small states, are balanced. The vote is single transferable.
The Indian President is a constitutional head, so the election keeps the office above a direct popular mandate.
France: any voter may vote. A second round between the top two follows if no one has a majority. The president who emerges leads the government and foreign policy.
A direct mandate can also polarise, which the two-round system only partly contains.
India's procedure protects a federal and nominal head. France's procedure creates a political one.

question_text: Discuss the role of the Election Commission of India in the light of the evolution of the Model Code of Conduct. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Election Commission and the Model Code
topics: Election Commission and the Model Code
keyPointers: The Code began as a party agreement, not as a statute
The Commission turned it into the rule of the campaign
Its role is to keep the party in office from using the state as a resource
The limit is that a code without a criminal tooth depends on the Commission's standing

points.text: The Model Code grew from a voluntary restraint into the Election Commission's main instrument during a campaign.
Parties first agreed it in Kerala and then nationally. The Commission expanded it to cover speeches, meetings, manifestos and the conduct of the government in power.
From the announcement of the election, a new scheme, a discretionary transfer and the use of public money for a campaign are policed under it.
The Commission issues notices, stops a speech's abuse and orders the administration.
Critics note that the Code is not itself a law, so a determined violator meets a rebuke more often than a disqualification. The Commission's authority has been the real sanction.
The Commission's role has been to make a moral code operate as the campaign's constitution.

question_text: Besides the welfare schemes, India needs deft management of inflation and unemployment to serve the poor and the underprivileged sections of the society. Discuss. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Inflation, jobs and the poor
topics: Inflation, jobs and the poor
subTopics: Inflation and unemployment as social justice
keyPointers: A scheme pays the poor; a price rise taxes them
Unemployment removes the wage that a scheme cannot replace
Macroeconomic management is therefore a welfare tool
The poor need both a transfer and a stable price and a job

points.text: Welfare schemes are not enough if prices and the lack of work undo them.
Food inflation hits a household that spends most of its income on food, even if a ration softens one part of the basket.
A jobless recovery leaves the underprivileged outside the growth that the schemes are funded by.
Managing inflation without crushing the very employment the poor need is the 'deft' part: supply of food, a careful credit stance, and works that hire.
A transfer helps. It does not hold a price down or create a regular wage.
Serving the poor requires the schemes and the two macro conditions the question names.

question_text: Do you agree with the view that increasing dependence on donor agencies for development reduces the importance of community participation in the development process? Justify your answer. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: Donors and community participation
topics: Donors and community participation
keyPointers: A donor can fund a project the community asked for, or replace the community
Dependence shifts the report from the village to the donor
Design, the clock and the indicator start to belong to the funder
The view is largely right, and it is not automatic

points.text: Yes, growing dependence on donors tends to shrink community participation, because the person who pays sets the question.
A project then answers the donor's format, timeline and definition of success.
The gram sabha is consulted late, or as a photograph, because the decision has already been logged.
Local knowledge about what will be maintained after the grant ends is the first casualty.
A donor that funds a community's own plan, and then leaves the choice of work to it, can do the opposite. That is the exception, and it requires the state to refuse a tied design.
Dependence reduces participation unless the money is deliberately made the servant of a local decision.

question_text: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 remains inadequate in promoting incentive-based system for children's education without generating awareness about the importance of schooling. Analyse. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: RTE and why enrolment is not enough
topics: RTE and why enrolment is not enough
keyPointers: The Act made schooling a right and built a duty on the state
An incentive brings a child in; a belief keeps the child there
Without awareness, the incentive is collected and the seat is empty
The Act is thin on the demand side of schooling

points.text: The RTE Act builds the supply of a school. It does not, by itself, build a family's reasons to use it.
Free seats, a neighbourhood school, no detention in the early years and a private school's quota are incentives of a kind.
A family that does not see a return, or that needs the child's labour, treats the incentive as a cash point.
Girls, migrants and children with a disability lose most where the community does not value the school.
Awareness, a teacher who stays, and a learning the parent can see are what make the legal incentive work.
The Act is inadequate on this point because a right that parents do not want to spend a day on remains unused.

question_text: How will I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE and USA) grouping transform India's position in global politics? (Answer in 250 words)
topic: I2U2 and India's position
topics: I2U2 and India's position
keyPointers: I2U2 puts India in a West Asian table with the United States and Israel
The agenda is food, water, energy and a project, not a military pact
It lifts India from a bilateral friend of each to a member of a small group
The transformation is real but limited to one region and one kind of cooperation

points.text: I2U2 changes India's position by seating it with the United States, Israel and the UAE on practical projects.
Food parks, water, clean energy and a corridor of investment give India a role in West Asian economic security.
The grouping shows that India's ties with Israel and the Gulf can run together, which an older politics thought impossible.
It does not make India a treaty ally, and it does not settle India's other balances, with Russia or in the Indo-Pacific.
Its value is a new minilateral habit: small, project-based, and useful.
India's position shifts from being courted by each capital separately to helping design a regional economic architecture.

question_text: ‘Clean energy is the order of the day.’ Describe briefly India's changing policy towards climate change in various international fora in the context of geopolitics. (Answer in 250 words)
topic: India's climate policy and geopolitics
topics: India's climate policy and geopolitics
keyPointers: India moved from defending a right to emit to offering a transition
Equity and a finance promise are still the condition
The shift tracks energy security and a geopolitical contest, not only a moral change
International fora are where India states both the offer and the condition

points.text: India's climate policy has changed from a defensive developing-country line to an active offer, without dropping equity.
At the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement India accepted a national contribution and later raised its non-fossil and intensity targets, including a net-zero year.
In the same halls it insists that finance and technology from those who emitted first are a condition, not a favour.
The International Solar Alliance and a green hydrogen push are geopolitical tools: they make India a rule-maker in the energy the world is moving to.
Choices at these fora are also about not being locked into one camp's supply chain.
Clean energy is the order of the day, and India is using that order to change its place, not only its fuel.
